extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for selecting news stories and preserving journalistic objectivity (including how competition, values, ideology, and organizational practices shape news judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of collusion/imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors avoid identical or obviously similar covers/leads to prevent the appearance of collusion and to escape accusations of a media conspiracy (example: magazines nervous after the Nixon Administration's attack on the media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without actual collusion, news organizations take pains not to appear collusive; this affects planning (e.g., refraining from fraternization about editorial plans) and can lead to secrecy about rival's cover plans. Imitation concerns vary by medium (less for television because leads are chosen late).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dyadic competition as quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists compare their own work directly with that of rivals within the same medium and format to evaluate performance and create consensus about key considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition provides the feedback journalists respect more than sparse audience feedback or supervisory comment. It helps determine which organization 'won' a contested story, though it is limited to peers in the same medium and format and thus may not capture more general substantive standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on a professional standard-setter (The New York Times)
rubrics_metrics.description: When cross-medium or broader substantive judgments are needed, journalists treat a leading outlet (notably The New York Times) as the standard setter and check how it covered a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and producers consult whether, where, and how the Times covered a topic; Times coverage influences television programs, magazines, back-of-the-book features, and review decisions. This functions as a profession-level benchmark beyond dyadic competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / Value exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism aims to be objective by excluding conscious personal values and ideology from story selection and production; values are excluded in the narrower sense of preference statements about nation and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials and commentary are often exempt, but for news selection the goal is to present facts (or attributed opinions) gathered 'objectively.' Objectivity is treated both as a professional ideal and as protection against criticism and censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity defined as intent and detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity is largely a matter of a journalist's intent (personal detachment) and use of similar fact-gathering methods validated by professional consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this definition, journalists may reach evaluative conclusions framed as 'subjective reactions' arising from objectively gathered facts. Training, avoidance of voting, and organizational incentives (rotation, high pay, status) are means to preserve detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from implications (disregard of effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists claim the right to disregard the implications or effects of the news when selecting and reporting stories; objectivity requires avoiding intended effects on society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This freedom prevents paralyzing self-censorship and allows timely reporting. However, it is bounded: journalists do sometimes alter or kill stories to protect innocent bystanders, national security, the war effort, or to prevent panic. They also selectively consider predictable implications when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness as a constraint when implications matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When implications cannot be ignored, journalists invoke fairness to guide choices; fairness is treated as a matter of intent regulated by enduring values and legal/professional rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness is determined by enduring values, libel laws, FCC rules, and balance considerations. Editors 'soften' writers' harsh judgments or pejorative adjectives to preserve fairness; conversely, editors rarely 'harden' judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of organizational mechanisms to preserve detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations employ structural practices (rotation of beats, separation of duties, assignment practices, rewarding getting the story) to maintain reporter detachment and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General reporters are moved quickly between stories; those on emotionally charged beats are rotated frequently. Story selectors who remain office-bound are naturally detached by duties. These practices reduce personal attachment that might bias coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of news and commentary / outlets for opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should avoid personal or advocacy journalism within news reporting; opinions and advocacy are expressed through separate channels (editorials, op-eds, daily commentary programs, cartoons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines and networks permit expression of strongly held views in designated formats (e.g., cartoons, opinion journals), thereby preserving the news function's claimed neutrality. Anchorpersons and reporters often have side platforms for commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance / exclusion of conscious ideology in newsrooms
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations prefer not to hire ideologically committed journalists for news roles because ideology is seen as an obstacle to neutral story selection and efficient production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hiring is nominally based on journalistic skill rather than political values, conformity pressures and organizational culture tend to drive out ideologues. Journalists commonly define 'ideology' as extreme political commitment, and thus marginalize those actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment practices prioritize journalistic skill over ideological screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiring decisions emphasize writing ability, college training, and related qualifications; explicit discussion of applicants' political values is avoided in interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples of writing can screen out candidates from purely ideological outlets on neutral grounds. Legal or managerial concerns (e.g., pending indictments) can override editorial interest in some hires, but generally values are not overtly probed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'house radicals' and 'house conservatives' as internal boundary markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Having identified internal figures labeled as radicals or conservatives serves latent functions: they allow colleagues to view themselves as non-ideological and define acceptable opinion boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House radicals were often hired to cover specific movements but tended to leave due to lifestyle and political isolation; house conservatives have persisted more readily because they fit culturally and politically inside the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological editing and story killing (rare but possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although uncommon, ideological considerations sometimes directly affect story selection or production—stories may be killed or toned down if they are judged to promote an ideology (example: a Time story killed because it 'made the Communists look too good').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideological editing is rare in domestic sections but may occur; more typically, editors tone down writers whose values conflict with organizational stances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Softening of language and selection of dramatic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors commonly 'soften' harsh writer judgments and select dramatic adjectives or pictures to vivify stories; cartoons and dramatic writing are tolerated as ways to liven copy, even when they risk unfairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Softening changes pejorative descriptors into less confrontational labels (e.g., 'reactionary politicians' to 'conservatives'). Editors rarely increase the harshness of a writer's judgment. Use of cartoons is seen as especially safe because they are reprints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative reporting exception for stronger attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reporters who have done the necessary legwork are permitted to attribute and identify liars more explicitly than routine reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because investigative reporting can substantiate allegations, it is an exception to the usual restraint on identifying dishonesty; routine reporters who lack proof are more cautious and rely on attributed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity as commercial protection and credential for audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity functions commercially: it is used to market uniform, sellable news to a diverse audience and to defend against accusations of bias which would erode credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Associated Press model and similar practices institutionalized objectivity partly to sell to politically diverse local outlets. Journalists also see objectivity as protecting the audience from misinformation by those with 'axes to grind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited value of audience feedback for news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience feedback is sparse and not regarded as valid or reliable for evaluating news judgment; journalists prefer peer competition and professional consensus as evaluative mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because audience metrics do not reveal the contours of professional quality and are often not timely or trusted, journalists rely more on comparisons with rivals and with standard-setters like The New York Times.
